blocks.text: Only snake venom is deadly (A. Sara 31b; see, however, §. 270). The snake lets the venom flow into the wound only after the bite [p. 235] (Sanhedrin 78a), and this venom causes burning pain, so that he who has been destined by Providence for death by fire is bitten by a snake (Sota 8b). Cattle bitten by a snake are also dangerous to eat, since the venom spreads through the whole body (Terumoth 8b). It very rarely bites a person when it is not provoked, but does so when it is trodden on (Berachoth 33a). It is vindictive (Joma 23a) and bites without deriving any enjoyment from it (Erachin 15a). It is therefore called רשע "evildoer" (Bechoroth 8a). There was also the proverb: "A person does not dwell with a snake in one basket," to describe a married couple one of whom is quarrelsome and malicious (Ketuboth 77a*). Before it bites, the snake emits a hissing sound (Sabbat 121b).

It eats earth (ibid. 85a); yet it is especially fond of water, wine and milk (Terumoth 8, 4), likewise of liquid fat (Beza 7b), which is why one should not consume such things if they have stood uncovered overnight in places where snakes dwell. This animal is especially greedy for wine, and it was once observed how a snake got the wine out of a narrow bottle by pouring water into the bottle, whereby the wine rose and overflowed (A, Sara 30a).
Aristotle already (loc. cit. 8, 6, 1) reports how snakes used to be caught by making them drunk with wine.
They also drink mixed wine, but not boiled wine that is only three days old (ibid. 30b**).

Snake venom varies in strength as well as in weight. That of a young snake is heavy and, when the snake discharges it into a liquid, sinks to the bottom of the vessel; that of an older snake remains suspended in the middle of the liquid; finally, that of an old snake stays floating on top, because it is light (A. Sara 30b). The venom of a young snake therefore [p. 236] kills only the one who drinks last from the vessel, i.e. who drinks the dregs (ibid.). The venom forms a coherent mass in the liquid, without dispersing through it (B. Kama 115b). The older the snake, the stronger it becomes, but in the same measure its venom becomes weaker in intensity (A. Sara 30b). Since the snake leaves fish brine, vinegar, honey, oil and fish sauce (מריים, Muria) untouched, these things may be consumed even if they have stood uncovered in places where snakes dwell; yet it is reported that once a snake drank of the fish brine too (Chulin 49b). It can also have fatal consequences if a bone splinter of a snake penetrates the sole of a person's foot (Pesachim 112b); yet it is known that the venom is located not in the teeth but in the salivary glands (§. 58); according to the Talmudic account, however, the snake's venom is effective even after its death, since those bones came from a snake killed by a cat, which, however, probably still requires proof *).

Remedies for snakebite are the following. One should put the bitten limb into a hen torn open alive (Joma 83b), or tear apart the embryo of a healthy white she-ass and lay it on the wound (Sabbat 109b); one may also lay crushed gnats on the wound (ibid. 77b). If someone has a snake in his body (Voigt l. c. 3. p. 11 relates such a case with a slow-worm, which was expelled by an emetic), he should eat hops (כשוחא) mixed with salt and then run three miles, whereby the snake is killed and passes out in pieces (טרונציץ, Tronçons) (Sabbat 109b).

A famous remedy against snake venom and against the venom of other animals was the חורייקי (Sabbat ibid); this is the Theriaca mentioned by Plin. (h. n. 20, 24, 100); this medicine consisted of the flesh of the snake prepared with various other ingredients, cf. Bondi; Or Ester p. 268.
On the snake mixture against scabies, see §. 292.
The snake has a very keen sense of hearing, so that it is scared away by the falling of drops from a vessel (A. Sara 30b).
[p. 237] It drinks by lapping and lets the liquid flow back again (Para 9, 3).
It can be tamed and reared (B. Kama 15b; Voigt l. c. 3. p. 51).
It copulates with bellies turned toward each other (Bechoroth 8a). The female admits the male even during gestation (ibid. 8b), and carries for seven years (ibid. 8a; cf., however, §. 17).
It lives in waterless cisterns (Chagiga 3a), also in houses, where it finds a dangerous enemy in cats (Pesachim 112b), since its venom does not harm the cat (Sabbat 128b), cf. §. 290 at the end.

The snake sometimes coils itself around a person, or lies on him, without harming him; in which case the person must roll it off himself very carefully and, if possible, throw it into water, so that he can then flee more easily (Sabbat 110a, with which compare Voigt l. c. 3. p. 50*).
If one boils a snake in olive oil, one obtains a mixture against scabies (Sabbat 77b and on this Aruch s.v. חף).
The Snake of Eretz Yisrael.
The snake living in Eretz Yisrael
נחש שבארץ ישראל

is the most dangerous, and may therefore be killed on the Sabbath (Sabbat 121b). The animal is not described more precisely; on the other hand, it is reported as a miracle that in Jerusalem itself a snake never harmed anyone (Aboth 5, 5).
